name: Spinal cord compression

matching.reasoningTemplate: Back pain with limb weakness and bladder dysfunction is cord compression until proven otherwise - image urgently.

redFlags: Time-critical for neurological recovery; high-dose steroids if malignant

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105
clinicalPearls: A horizontally demarcated sensory level (identified by moving a pinprick or cold stimulus up the trunk) below which sensory, motor and autonomic function is impaired is the hallmark of a cord lesion; for the spinothalamic tract the true level may sit one to two segments above the clinically detected level (p.3603).
The upper border of sensory loss often lies one or two vertebrae BELOW the actual site of compression, so the radiographic target may be higher than the clinical level suggests (p.631).

Pain is usually the first symptom of metastatic compression and can precede neurological signs by days to months; it characteristically worsens when supine/recumbent and at night, helping distinguish it from degenerative disk pain which is often relieved by lying down (pp.631, 768, 3605).
Lhermitte's sign (an electric tingling shooting down the back and limbs on neck flexion/extension) can be an EARLY clue to cervical cord compression (p.631).
Loss of bowel/bladder control is usually a LATE feature; motor and sensory loss typically precede sphincter disturbance (p.631).
Useful trunk sensory landmarks for localising a thoracic level are the nipples (T4) and umbilicus (T10) (p.3604).

Spinal column infection (osteomyelitis/abscess) characteristically crosses the disk space to involve the adjacent vertebral body, whereas tumour tends to respect the disk space - a distinguishing imaging feature (p.3605).
Vertebral collapse is not a reliable marker of malignancy - about 20% of collapses, especially in older and postmenopausal patients, are due to osteoporosis rather than tumour (p.632).
Pedicle erosion (the 'winking owl' sign) is the earliest plain-film sign of vertebral tumour, but plain films are insensitive and a normal film does not exclude malignancy (p.632).
harrison.pathophysiology: Because the cord packs nearly the entire motor output and sensory input of the trunk and limbs into a small cross-section, even a small compressive mass causes disproportionately severe, often reversible-if-treated-early, deficits (p.3559). In neoplastic compression, metastases lodge in the vertebral body or pedicle (the axial skeleton is rich in marrow); the enlarging deposit compresses the underlying dura, or a paravertebral mass (lymphoma, myeloma, paediatric tumours) extends through the intervertebral foramen into the canal. Expanding extradural tumour injures axons and myelin mechanically and compromises blood flow, producing ischaemia and infarction (pp.589, 3563). In spinal epidural abscess, as the collection expands it causes additional cord damage through venous congestion and thrombosis, so that once weakness appears deterioration can be rapid and irreversible (p.3606). The thoracic spine is the commonest site of metastatic compression (~70%), followed by lumbosacral (~20%) and cervical (~10%) (p.631).
additionalDifferentials: Intradural extramedullary tumours (meningioma, neurofibroma/schwannoma) - usually slow-growing and benign; long symptom duration favours an intradural origin (p.3606)

Intramedullary lesions (ependymoma, haemangioblastoma, low-grade astrocytoma, rarely metastasis) - present with poorly localised burning pain and SACRAL SPARING rather than radicular pain (p.3604, 3606)

Cervical spondylotic / degenerative cervical myelopathy - osteophytes, ossified posterior longitudinal ligament/ligamentum flavum, disk degeneration; insidious, stepwise; early signs are subtle (paraesthesia, loss of hand dexterity, 'clumsiness') (p.173)
Acute spondylytic myelopathy from hyperextension injury on a pre-existing stenotic canal, sometimes producing a central cord syndrome (p.3606)
Conus medullaris syndrome - saddle anaesthesia (S3-S5), early prominent bladder/bowel dysfunction with lax anal tone, preserved leg strength (p.3604)
infectionMimics: Spinal epidural abscess - midline spinal/neck pain, fever and progressive limb weakness; mostly Staphylococcus aureus (consider MRSA), with gram-negative bacilli, streptococci, anaerobes and fungi less commonly; risk factors include diabetes, IV drug use, alcoholism, renal failure, malignancy, HIV and recent spinal surgery/anaesthesia/trauma (pp.3606-3607)
Vertebral osteomyelitis / diskitis - neurological deficit in about a third of cases, mostly mediated by epidural abscess; fever may be absent, especially in cervical disease (pp.131, 1105)
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease) with epidural extension - an important cause in the developing world (p.3607)
Infectious noncompressive myelitis to consider once compression excluded (VZV, HSV, CMV, HIV, HTLV-1, Borrelia, Listeria, syphilis, Mycoplasma) (p.3603)
nonInfectiousMimics: Spinal epidural haematoma - acute focal/radicular pain then cord or conus signs; predisposed by anticoagulation, trauma, tumour or blood dyscrasias, occasionally post-LP or epidural anaesthesia (p.3607)
Hematomyelia - acute painful transverse myelopathy from intramedullary haemorrhage (trauma, vascular malformation, vasculitis, coagulopathy) (p.3607)
Spinal cord infarction / anterior spinal artery syndrome - sudden myelopathy without antecedent pain, with preserved vibration/position sense (pp.3604-3605)
Radiation myelopathy, neoplastic leptomeningitis and spinal lipomatosis (p.631)
Subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12 deficiency), copper deficiency (p.3602)
Inflammatory/demyelinating myelopathy - multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, sarcoidosis (p.3602)
additionalInvestigations: MRI with gadolinium centred on the suspected level is the initial procedure; imaging the entire spine is important because up to ~40% with compression at one level have asymptomatic epidural metastases elsewhere (and multiple epidural deposits are present in ~25%) (pp.632, 3605)
CT myelography reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI promptly or have non-diagnostic MRI (pp.632, 768)
ESR and CRP are valuable for excluding spinal infection (raised in ~98-100% of vertebral osteomyelitis) (p.1105)
Blood cultures (positive in over half of epidural abscess cases); image-guided or open biopsy/aspiration when cultures are negative (pp.1105, 3607)
If cord compression suspected but only radicular symptoms without myelopathy, imaging may safely be deferred 24-48 h - but suspected myelopathic compression is imaged immediately (p.3605)
In compression from an unknown primary, a simple workup (chest imaging, mammography, PSA, abdominal CT) often reveals the malignancy (p.632)
redFlags: Established motor deficit (paraplegia/quadriplegia) present >12 h rarely improves, and beyond 48 h the prognosis for meaningful motor recovery is poor - urgency is measured in hours (p.3606)

Autonomic dysfunction (decreased anal tone, reduced perineal sensation, distended bladder, absent anal wink or bulbocavernosus reflex) signals cord involvement and is an unfavourable prognostic sign (p.631)
Once weakness appears in spinal epidural abscess, progression can be rapid and irreversible (p.3606)
Recent-onset persistent thoracic back pain in a cancer patient is suspicious for vertebral metastasis (the thoracic spine is rarely involved by spondylosis) (p.3605)
Pain crescendo pattern, pain aggravated by cough/Valsalva/recumbency, and Lhermitte's sign warrant urgent imaging (p.632)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome is strongly time- and function-dependent: treatment is most successful in patients who are still ambulatory and have intact sphincter control when therapy begins, and a good response is expected in those ambulatory at presentation - treatment usually prevents new weakness and up to a third regain some motor function (pp.632, 3606). Motor deficits fixed for more than 12 h seldom improve, and beyond 48 h substantial recovery is unlikely (p.3606). For spinal epidural abscess, prompt diagnosis and treatment allow significant recovery in up to two-thirds, but surgery is unlikely to reverse deficits fixed for more than a few days (p.3607). Recovery from paraparesis is better after surgery than radiotherapy alone, though survival may be short with widespread metastatic disease (p.768).
pitfalls: Mistaking a myelopathy for polyneuropathy or Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending paraesthesias suggest neuropathy, but a sharply demarcated sensory level plus bladder disturbance points to a cord origin (pp.213, 3605).

Acute severe transverse lesions cause initial FLACCID weakness and areflexia ('spinal shock') that can be misread as anterior horn cell disease or acute polyneuropathy before hyperreflexia supervenes over days to weeks (p.3604).

Cauda equina syndrome (low back/radicular pain, saddle/perineal sensory loss, asymmetric leg weakness, sphincter and sexual dysfunction, lost ankle/bulbocavernosus/anal reflexes) reflects nerve-root rather than cord compression and must be distinguished from conus and cord syndromes - mass lesions low in the canal often produce a mixed picture (pp.132, 632, 3604).
Gadolinium enhancement can deceptively 'normalise' vertebral metastases by raising their signal to that of normal marrow on MRI (p.3605).
Cervical osteomyelitis/epidural abscess may present without fever, delaying recognition - keep it in mind for neck pain with IV drug use, immunosuppression or diabetes (p.131).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames management decisions for malignant compression using the NOMS framework (Memorial Sloan Kettering): Neurologic status (degree of epidural compression, myelopathy, functional radiculopathy), Oncologic status (tumour radiosensitivity), Mechanical stability of the spine, and Systemic factors; high-grade epidural compression from a radioresistant tumour favours separation surgery followed by stereotactic body radiotherapy (pp.589-590). Clinically, prognosis is best stratified by ambulatory and sphincter status at presentation and by duration of any motor deficit (p.3606).
